passage: The agriculture diploma results came out on the same afternoon in Hoshangabad. Himani had missed the merit list by a few ranks. She read it twice, sighed, and by evening had pinned next year's form to the wall. 'One exam,' she said. 'Not the end of the world.' Her cousin Vikas had missed it too. Over tea she told him the same thing, cheerfully. 'Chill, na. Next year.' He nodded. For three days after that he didn't come to the dairy where they both helped. On the fourth, Himani found him by the canal, throwing stones. She almost said 'chill' again. Instead she sat down. 'I think I assumed it hit you the way it hit me. How bad is it, really?' Vikas threw another stone. 'Bad,' he said. 'Papa had already told everyone I'd get in.' She stayed till dark, mostly listening.

qa.a: Next year's form.

'I think I've been assuming you're like me about criticism. Are you?' A long pause. The door opened. 'No,' Mei said, eyes red. 'I've been thinking about leaving the course.' During today's film about an elephant calf that lost its herd, Tenzin cried hard and couldn't stop even after it ended. passage: Santiago noticed things about Nkechi that the others at their Manchester school didn't. When Mr. Hale slammed a book on the desk, she flinched as if she'd been hit. At lunch she ate on the library steps, not in the roaring canteen. When the group decided to throw her a surprise party in the form room, with poppers and everyone jumping out, Santiago felt his stomach drop. 'She'll hate that,' he said. 'Don't be boring,' Jake said. Santiago didn't argue. But the night before, he messaged Nkechi: 'Heads-up: they're planning a surprise for you tomorrow at break. Loud. Wanted you to know.' Nkechi wrote back: 'Thank you. Really.' Next day she walked in smiling, ready for it, and asked them to skip the poppers. They did.

qa.q: Where did Nkechi eat lunch?
qa.a: On the library steps.

qa.q: What did Santiago feel when the group planned the surprise?
qa.a: Santiago felt his stomach drop, worried the loud surprise would upset Nkechi.

qa.q: Why was Santiago's heads-up a kind choice?
qa.a: It kept the celebration but let Nkechi prepare, so she walked in ready and could ask them to skip the poppers.

qa.q: What was the next day like for Nkechi because of the message?
qa.a: Nkechi felt grateful and ready, walking in smiling instead of being startled.

grounding: Shows a classmate noticing a sensitive peer who flinches at loud noises and needs quiet, and giving her a heads-up before a surprise.

passage: In the chemistry lab, Mr. Bhatt shouted when someone knocked over a beaker, and Tushar saw Indu jump so hard she dropped her pen. She went pale and didn't speak for the rest of the class. Tushar had sat beside her all year. He'd noticed she ate lunch in a corner of the library, not the noisy canteen, and that she hated the fire-drill bell. At lunch he went to the library too. 'Mind if I eat here? It's quieter.' She nodded. A boy from their class passed and mimicked her jump. Tushar felt a flash of anger. 'Not funny,' he said, and the boy shrugged and left. Before the bell, Tushar said, 'Heads-up, there's a fire drill after fourth period. Sir told us.' Indu let out a breath. 'Thanks. That really helps.'

qa.q: What did Indu drop when Mr. Bhatt shouted?
qa.a: Her pen.

qa.q: What did Tushar feel when the boy mimicked Indu's jump?
qa.a: Tushar felt a flash of anger, protective of Indu.

qa.q: Which of Tushar's small kindnesses mattered most, and why?
qa.a: The heads-up about the fire drill, because it let Indu prepare for a noise she hates.

qa.q: What was the lab like for Indu?
qa.a: Indu was startled and shaken by the shouting, going pale and silent for the rest of the class.

grounding: Shows a classmate who notices a sensitive peer flinch at raised voices and need quiet, and offers company, a heads-up and a stop to teasing.

passage:
Dear Binita,
I've been meaning to say sorry since Tuesday. When Ma'am slammed the register and you jumped, and some of us laughed, I laughed too. I saw your face after. I felt awful all evening.
I've been noticing things since. You eat in the art room, not the canteen. You go quiet when the bus gets loud. I think noise hits you harder than it hits me, and that isn't something to laugh at.
So here's what I can do, if you want: I'll text you a heads-up when I hear about surprise tests or the fire drill. I'll eat in the art room on Thursdays if you'd like company, or leave you alone if you wouldn't. And if anyone teases you, this time I'll say something.
Dilnaz

qa.q: Where does Binita eat lunch?
qa.a: In the art room.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel after laughing on Tuesday?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt awful and guilty all evening after seeing Binita's face.

qa.q: Which of Dilnaz's offers are most useful, and why?
qa.a: Heads-ups before surprise tests and drills, and speaking up against teasing; they make noisy surprises and mockery less likely to hurt.

qa.q: How might Binita feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Binita would probably feel relieved and seen, knowing a classmate noticed and wants to help without pushing.

grounding: Shows a classmate who notices a sensitive peer startled by noise and needing quiet, apologises for laughing, and offers heads-ups and no teasing.

passage: On the walk home from college in Pune, Akash stopped dead on the pavement. An old man was playing a sarangi outside the bank, and the sound went straight through him; his eyes stung, and he stood there for three songs while Rashmi waited, amused. 'You feel everything, don't you?' she said. He did. The monsoon smell, a stranger's kindness at the bus stop, a good line in a poem. But the same week, when his project group argued over deadlines, the shouting felt as if it were inside his ribs. He couldn't sleep, and lost a whole evening just recovering. That Sunday he tried something new. He blocked two hours in his planner, marked them 'quiet', and spent them by the lake. 'It's not weakness,' he told Rashmi later. 'It's the same wiring. I just need to recharge it.'

qa.q: What was the old man playing?
qa.a: A sarangi.

qa.q: How did Akash feel when his project group argued?
qa.a: He felt the conflict sharply, as if the shouting were inside his ribs, and couldn't sleep.

qa.q: What did Akash do on Sunday, and why does it help?
qa.a: He blocked two quiet hours by the lake; scheduled downtime lets him recover from how intensely he feels.

qa.q: How does Rashmi see Akash stopping for the sarangi?
qa.a: Rashmi is amused and affectionate, noticing that he feels everything deeply.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels music and kindness intensely and conflict sharply, and learns to schedule downtime and see sensitivity as depth.

passage:
'Veerji, you're crying at a sunset again?'
Baljeet laughed and wiped his eyes. 'It's pink, Mehak. Look at it.'
'You cried at the wedding band too. And when the chai-wala gave that kid a free biscuit.'
'I know.' He sat on the terrace wall. 'It's wonderful. And it's terrible. That group presentation last week? Arvind snapped at me in front of everyone and I felt it for three days.'
'Three days?'
'Three. Kept replaying it.'
Mehak sat beside him. 'So what, you'll stop feeling things?'
'No. I've started keeping Saturday mornings empty. No plans, no calls. Just walking by the canal.'
'And that works?'
'It helps me come back. The same feeling makes me good at design, Mehak. I just need to refill.'
She bumped his shoulder. 'Okay, sensitive genius. Enjoy your sunset.'

qa.q: Who snapped at Baljeet?
qa.a: Arvind, in front of everyone.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel after Arvind snapped at him?
qa.a: He felt hurt for three days, replaying it over and over.

qa.q: Why does Baljeet keep Saturday mornings empty?
qa.a: It is scheduled downtime that helps him recover from how sharply he feels conflict.

qa.q: How does Mehak see her brother's sensitivity?
qa.a: She teases him affectionately but accepts it, calling him a 'sensitive genius'.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels beauty and kindness intensely and conflict sharply, scheduling downtime and seeing his sensitivity as depth.

passage: I used to think something was wrong with me. I'm Shalini. The first time I heard a live veena concert, I had to leave the hall because I was crying too hard. A friend's small kindness could keep me warm for a week. But the same thing that made music so huge made my final-year deadlines feel like a wall falling on me. When Ujjwal and I clashed over our thesis chapters, I lay awake three nights. Ujjwal said once, not unkindly, 'You feel everything at volume ten.' It took me a while to stop hearing that as an insult. What changed was small: I started keeping one evening a week empty, and I stopped saving all the hard work for the last two days. I still cry at concerts. I just don't think it's weakness any more. It's depth, and depth needs rest.

qa.q: What made Shalini leave the concert hall?
qa.a: Crying too hard at a live veena concert.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel after clashing with Ujjwal over the thesis chapters?
qa.a: Shalini felt it sharply and anxiously, lying awake three nights.

qa.q: What two changes helped Shalini?
qa.a: Keeping one evening a week empty, and not leaving all the hard work for the last two days.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have meant by 'You feel everything at volume ten'?
qa.a: Ujjwal seems to have been describing Shalini honestly, not unkindly, though at first it sounded like an insult.

grounding: Shows a young adult who experiences music and kindness intensely and conflict and deadlines sharply, and learns to schedule downtime and see sensitivity as depth.

passage: Vandana had turned down the higher-paying job in the open-plan office in Gurgaon, and her uncle still hadn't forgiven her. Instead she'd taken a translation post at a small publisher in Noida: her own corner, a door that closed, deadlines she could plan around. On Monday her editor, Divyansh, asked her to help at the book-fair stall for three days. Her chest tightened; crowds wore her down fast. But she didn't say no automatically. 'I'll do the first morning and the author talk,' she said. 'Not all three days. I'll need the afternoon after to recover.' She didn't apologise. Divyansh nodded. 'Fair.' At the fair she introduced two authors, answered questions, and left at two, as planned. The next day, rested, she finished a whole chapter. It was the right kind of stretch.

qa.q: Where did Vandana take the translation post?
qa.a: At a small publisher in Noida.

qa.q: What did Vandana feel when asked to help at the book-fair stall?
qa.a: Her chest tightened, knowing crowds wear her down, though she still wanted to consider it.

qa.q: How did Vandana stretch herself without overloading?
qa.a: She agreed to the first morning and the author talk, asked for the afternoon after to recover, and didn't apologise for it.

qa.q: How might Vandana's uncle see her choice of job?
qa.a: He seems disappointed and unforgiving, seeing only the higher pay she turned down, not how well the quiet job suits her.

grounding: Shows a sensitive young adult who chose work with control over noise and pace, keeps boundaries without apology, and still stretches herself gently.

passage:
'You're leaving the reception already?' Lalit caught Gurleen's arm by the door.
'I've been here three hours, Lalit. I danced, I met every aunty, I gave the speech.'
'And now?'
'Now my head's buzzing. That's my signal. I'm going to sit in the car with the window down for twenty minutes.'
'People will say you're rude.'
'Some might. I'm not going to apologise for needing quiet.' She smiled. 'Remember last year? I stayed till two and then couldn't work properly for three days.'
'You cried at the office.'
'Exactly. So, new plan. Work from home twice a week, no meetings before ten, and breaks at parties.'
'And you'll come back in?'
'For the cake. I always come back for the cake.'
Twenty minutes later she did, cheeks cool, and danced with their Nani.

qa.q: What did Gurleen give at the reception?
qa.a: The speech.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she wanted to leave?
qa.a: Her head was buzzing and she felt overwhelmed, which she read as a signal to rest.

qa.q: What does Gurleen's new plan include?
qa.a: Working from home twice a week, no meetings before ten, and breaks at parties.

qa.q: Why might Lalit worry about people calling Gurleen rude?
qa.a: Lalit cares what the family thinks, and is torn between the guests and his sister's needs.

grounding: Shows a sensitive young adult who treats overwhelm as a signal to rest, doesn't apologise for needing quiet, and shapes work and social life to fit.

passage: Two years ago I was a nurse on an emergency ward, and I loved the patients and hated the noise. I'm Indu. By the end of each shift I felt turned inside out. I cried in the changing room and apologised to everyone for 'being weak'. My friend Nandini said, 'You're not weak. You're in the wrong room.' So I made a slow change. I applied to the palliative care unit: quieter, slower, more time with each family. I still have hard days. Now, when my chest goes tight and every sound sharpens, I take my break and don't say sorry for it. I also say yes to things that scare me a little. Last month I gave a talk to thirty nursing students. My hands shook. But I did it, and then I went home and sat in the quiet.

qa.q: Which unit did Indu apply to?
qa.a: The palliative care unit.

qa.q: How did Indu feel at the end of emergency ward shifts?
qa.a: Indu felt turned inside out and exhausted, crying in the changing room.

qa.q: How does Indu balance rest and stretching now?
qa.a: By taking breaks without apologising when overwhelmed, while still saying yes to scary things like the talk to thirty students.

qa.q: What did Nandini see that Indu didn't?
qa.a: Nandini saw that the problem was the noisy setting, not weakness: 'You're in the wrong room.'

grounding: Shows a sensitive young adult who moves to work with calmer noise and pace, takes rest without apology when overwhelmed, and still stretches gently.
